title: Your own split
topic: Size your buffer with your bank data

steps.title: "Notgroschen first. Then let the rest wait."
steps.body: Lena's rule: three months of costs stay in Tagesgeld, ready any day. Money for Mia at 18 doesn't need to be reachable tomorrow. Her rule, not a recipe: a buffer sized by her [[emergency-fund|Notgroschen]] and her family.

steps.prompt: Why does Lena size her buffer in months of costs, not in a round amount?
options: Because the buffer has to cover life while an income is missing
Because round amounts earn less interest
steps.explanation: A buffer buys time. Months of costs tell you how much time, whatever the family spends.

steps.prompt: Lena keeps much more than her buffer in Tagesgeld for 20 years. What's the cost?
options: If interest stays below inflation, it slowly buys less
The bank charges a fee for large balances
steps.explanation: Safe money is safe from falls, not from [[inflation]]. Over long periods, the gap between interest and prices adds up.

t1.title: "Emergency money first. The rest can wait."
t1.body: Lena's rule: money for three months of costs stays in the savings account. Mia's money is for when she is 18, so it doesn't need to be ready tomorrow. This is Lena's rule, not a rule for everyone.

q1.prompt: Why does Lena count her emergency money in months?
options: It must pay for life while one salary is missing
q1.explanation: Emergency money buys time. Months tell you how much time.

q2.prompt: Lena keeps a lot more than she needs in the savings account for 20 years. What does it cost?
options: If interest is lower than price rises, it buys less over time
Nothing, the number never goes down
q2.explanation: Safe money doesn't go down, but [[inflation]] still makes it worth less.
